A4 = an OPTIONAL-WRAPPED user-defined class reference, with A1 = copy of an optional reference and A8 = the allocation may not happen at all. `Node`'s declaration is outside the fragment, so its `init(id:)` may be FAILABLE; `first` and `second` are then `Node?`, the fragment still compiles because `===` is declared on `AnyObject?`, and `same` is true because two absent values compare identical - the fragment reports 'the same object' although no object exists. WITNESS: semantic-compression/probes/witnesses/F04.P3/swift/V2_failable_init_optional_identity.swift, measured fragment byte-identical, with `init?(id: Int32) { return nil }`; it builds under the frozen recipe and the observer prints `optionalIdentity=true`. Material on dimension 8 (the values compared are optionals, not references), dimension 6 (no instance is allocated) and dimension 9 (the same printed `true` now means something else). || EXCLUDED CLASSES with citations and refutations. A4 = a VALUE type (struct or enum) is NOT REALIZABLE: `===` is declared only for `AnyObject?`, and the refutation witness semantic-compression/probes/witnesses/F04.P3/swift/REFUT_identity_operator_needs_class.swift is REJECTED by swiftc - this is the branch the fragment closes with a single operator, and it is why Swift's count here is low rather than high. A1 = MOVE/CONSUME is excluded because Swift requires the `consume` operator to be written (Swift Reference, 'Expressions > Consume Expression') and because `first` is read after `[first]`. A2 = 'state referred to by the operand may be mutated' is not realizable INSIDE the fragment: the only calls are an initializer, an array-literal construction and `===`, and the fragment holds no writable access to anything already existing; a user `init` may of course mutate state elsewhere, which is charged as a locality lookup and as a hidden item rather than as a branch (Rule 1.4.7). A8 = 'destruction/cleanup may run here' is not realizable at the span: both bindings are still live when `same` is produced, so no release point falls inside the fragment. A1 = non-call/token substitution is NOT REALIZABLE, LOW-B-BY-ABSENCE (no preprocessor; Swift macros need a marker plus a plugin module the single-file recipe does not build, Rule 1.3.3).

locality_detail.hop: type declaration (TYPE) - `final class Node { var id: Int32; init(id:) }`, which the probe places outside the measured fragment
locality_detail.required_for_fact: type_and_representation and allocation_copy_move_borrow_destroy. The fragment's `===` pins that `Node` is a class, but not WHICH class: whether `init(id:)` is failable (and therefore whether `first` is a `Node` or a `Node?`, and whether an instance is allocated at all) is decided only by the declaration, as the V2 witness shows. The greedy step selects it first because it resolves two facts.

locality_detail.hop: standard-library declaration (SIG) - `func === (lhs: AnyObject?, rhs: AnyObject?) -> Bool`
locality_detail.required_for_fact: aliasing_writable_aliasing. That the comparison is reference identity rather than a value comparison, and that the two implicit promotions it applies preserve identity, is stated by this declaration and its documentation; TSPL introduces the operator but the operand type - and hence the optional behaviour the V2 witness exposes - is in the library declaration. Under Rule 2.2.2 a standard-library declaration is a hop on the same terms as a user declaration. `value_vs_storage`, `lifetime_resource_effect` and the remaining facts follow from Swift's universal reference-type and ARC rules and add no hop (Rule 2.2.3).

hidden_items.why: Both operands of `===` undergo an implicit existential erasure to `AnyObject` and an implicit optional promotion to `AnyObject?`, with no cast, constructor or annotation written at the site (Swift standard library, `===`; TSPL 'The Basics > Optionals'). The conversion changes the set of representable values in a way that is observable at this very site: once the operands are optionals, two ABSENT values compare identical, so the fragment can report 'the same object' when no object exists - demonstrated by semantic-compression/probes/witnesses/F04.P3/swift/V2_failable_init_optional_identity.swift, which prints `optionalIdentity=true`. LED fails because nothing local distinguishes the promoted case from the reference case.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H4 - Implicit allocation, copy, move, destruction, or cleanup
hidden_items.why: The instance created at `Node(id: 5)` and the buffer created at `[first]` are both reference-counted, and their release - together with any `deinit` the class declares - runs at a point no token in the fragment names (TSPL 'Automatic Reference Counting'; 'Deinitialization'). A `deinit` is user-visible code, so this is not the GC-with-no-observable-effect case that methodology 04 section 1.4's H4 exclusion covers, and the retain/release traffic itself is the event methodology 03 Rule 1.2.2.b hands to this metric rather than to Determinacy. The allocations themselves are NOT counted: they are named by a constructor call and a container literal, which H4's exclusion list covers explicitly.

determinacy_enumeration: P1 (copy / derived handle) x M0 x E0 - the callee receives the value and nothing caller-observable changes. Under Swift's calling convention a non-owned parameter is passed as a borrow rather than a deep copy, but for a copy-on-write value type no observer in the caller can distinguish 'the callee got an independent copy' from 'the callee got a read-only borrow': a write on either side copies first. The corpus's two mandated outcomes 'callee cannot observe caller's object at all' and 'a copy was made so no caller-visible change is possible' therefore merge into this single vector under Rule 1.4.5, and 'callee may read but not write it' (P4 x M0 x E0) merges with it too, the merge being demonstrated rather than asserted by semantic-compression/probes/witnesses/F05.P1/swift/REFUT_E1_retain_by_value_cow.swift, where a callee that stores the argument in a global and writes it after the call leaves the caller's read at 1 (`result=1 savedAfterWrite=77`). WITNESS for the vector itself: the frozen probe file, built with `swiftc -O` and run; output 1.

P2 (converting copy) x M2 x E0 - an implicit ARRAY-TO-POINTER conversion at the argument position hands the callee an `UnsafePointer<Int>` into the array's own element buffer, through which it WRITES elements that the post-call read observes, while the operand remains usable. WITNESS: semantic-compression/probes/witnesses/F05.P1/swift/V2_unsafepointer_conversion_writes_caller.swift, measured fragment byte-identical, with `func f(_ v: UnsafePointer<Int>)` that does `UnsafeMutablePointer(mutating: v)[0] = 99`; it builds under the frozen recipe and the observer prints `callee sees element0 = 1` then `99` - the caller's element 0 changed through a bare, unmarked call site. Material on dimensions 1, 2 and 9. E remains E0: the standard library specifies the pointer produced by this conversion as valid only for the duration of the call, so retention beyond it is not a supported outcome (see the exclusion below).

P2 (converting copy) x M0 x E0 - an implicit conversion hands the callee an object of a DIFFERENT type than the operand's while preserving value semantics: optional promotion to `[Int]?`, or existential erasure to `Any`. Nothing is written at the argument position for either. WITNESS: semantic-compression/probes/witnesses/F05.P1/swift/REFUT_P2_optional_promotion.swift (the file name predates this adjudication; it is a positive witness), fragment byte-identical, with `func f(_ v: [Int]?)`; observer output `optional-promoted: Optional([1, 2, 3])` then `1`. Material on dimensions 4 and 8: the callee receives a differently represented object, which is exactly what axis P2 asks. || EXCLUDED CLASSES with citations and refutations. P3 (MOVE/CONSUME) is NOT REALIZABLE: a `consuming` parameter is legal, but because the fragment reads `x` after the call the compiler must copy rather than consume, and the operand stays valid - refutation semantic-compression/probes/witnesses/F05.P1/swift/REFUT_P3_consuming.swift, with `func f(_ v: consuming [Int])`, builds and prints 1 (Swift Reference, 'Declarations > Parameter Modifiers'). P5 (DEFERRED) is NOT REALIZABLE: `@autoclosure` defers the ARGUMENT, not the callee's body, and the deferred expression here is a read of a local constant with no side effect, so no observer program distinguishes it - refutation semantic-compression/probes/witnesses/F05.P1/swift/REFUT_P5_autoclosure.swift builds and prints 1, the same result (Rule 1.2.1; Swift Reference, 'Attributes > autoclosure'). P6 (NON-CALL) is NOT REALIZABLE, LOW-B-BY-ABSENCE: Swift has no preprocessor and its macros require a marker in the source plus a separate plugin module the single-file frozen recipe does not build (Rule 1.4.8, Rule 1.3.3). M1 (the callee writes the caller's VARIABLE) is NOT REALIZABLE: writable access to a caller's variable requires `&` at the call site (Swift Reference, 'Expressions > In-Out Expression'), and `x` is a `let` in any case - refutation: replacing `f`'s parameter with `inout [Int]` makes swiftc reject the unchanged call site. M3 (the callee replaces or RESIZES the sequence observable through `x`) is NOT REALIZABLE for the same reason: resizing requires either `inout` access or a mutating method on the caller's own binding. E1 (RETENTION beyond the call) is NOT REALIZABLE: for the by-value readings the callee retains its own copy-on-write copy, which the caller cannot observe (refutation semantic-compression/probes/witnesses/F05.P1/swift/REFUT_E1_retain_by_value_cow.swift, `result=1 savedAfterWrite=77`), and for the pointer reading the standard library specifies the converted pointer as valid only for the duration of the call, so a retained pointer is a documented misuse rather than an outcome - refutation semantic-compression/probes/witnesses/F05.P1/swift/REFUT_E1_pointer_retention.swift stores the pointer in a global and prints 1, with no caller-observable effect.

hidden_items.why: A distinct normative rule from the one above, at the same site: a non-optional value is accepted where an optional is expected (TSPL 'The Basics > Optionals') and a concrete type is erased into `Any`/a protocol existential (Swift Reference, 'Types'). Either changes the object the callee receives - witnessed by semantic-compression/probes/witnesses/F05.P1/swift/REFUT_P2_optional_promotion.swift, whose callee prints `Optional([1, 2, 3])` - and neither is written at the argument position. Two distinct registry rules at one site are two distinct events under methodology 04 section 1.3.2.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H3 - Overload or dynamic dispatch not locally evident
hidden_items.why: `f` may be overloaded, and its declaration is outside the local site (methodology 04 section 0.7), so the set of candidate bodies compatible with `f(x)` has cardinality >= 2. The candidate-equivalence exclusion is not available on the record: the witnesses above show candidates that differ on whether the caller's elements change and on what the callee receives.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H4 - Implicit allocation, copy, move, destruction, or cleanup
hidden_items.why: Passing `x` performs reference-counting traffic on the array's buffer, and if the callee stores the argument the buffer becomes shared so that a LATER write on either side allocates a fresh buffer and copies every element (Swift standard library, `Array`: copy-on-write). Nothing at `f(x)` marks that the value passed is a shared handle rather than an independent one. Methodology 03 Rule 1.2.2 removes this from Determinacy as retain/release traffic the runtime may elide, and Rule 1.2.2.b directs it here rather than letting it disappear.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H9 - Hidden side effects on existing state
hidden_items.why: `f` is an ordinary function with no effect annotation of any kind: Swift marks throwing and suspending calls at the call site but has no marker for reading or writing global, static or actor-external state, so `f(x)` may read and write module-level state named nowhere in the local site. Demonstrated by semantic-compression/probes/witnesses/F05.P1/swift/REFUT_E1_retain_by_value_cow.swift, whose callee assigns to a module-level `var saved` through the identical call site. Not already assigned to H1-H8: this is the effect on state, not a conversion, a dispatch choice, a resource event or a failure edge.
